strengths: The core idea is clean and well-motivated: formulating post-pruning error compensation as an Orthogonal Procrustes problem provides a principled, closed-form (SVD-based) solution that explicitly preserves output geometry (norms, angles), addressing a real limitation of unconstrained least-squares fitting under small calibration sets.

The variance-aware column scoring is a simple, low-overhead extension of the widely-used Wanda-sp heuristic and is well motivated by the connection between input variance and principal output directions.

The method is easy to integrate into existing pruning pipelines (no architectural changes, drop-in after column pruning) and has modest computational overhead (SVD of a d_out x d_out matrix), which is a practical strength.

Reasonably thorough ablations are provided: comparison of LS vs. rotation-only vs. rotation+scale compensation (Figure 2), and an ablation on which sub-layers (o_proj/down_proj) benefit most from compensation (Table 3), along with efficiency/parameter-count analysis (Table 4).
Perplexity results show a fairly consistent trend of improvement over WANDA-sp and are competitive with or better than FLAP across pruning ratios.
weaknesses: Experiments are conducted on a single, relatively dated model (LLaMA-7B) with no validation on larger or more modern LLM families (e.g., Llama-2/3, Mistral, Qwen), which severely limits confidence in the generality/significance of the method for a top-tier venue in 2026.

Baselines are limited to WANDA-sp and FLAP; no comparison against other relevant structured-pruning or geometry-preserving approaches mentioned in related work (e.g., LLM-Pruner, SliceGPT), despite SliceGPT being explicitly discussed as a related orthogonal-transformation method — an empirical comparison would substantially strengthen the paper.

The benchmark accuracy results (Table 2) are mixed rather than consistently favorable: FLAP outperforms RCPU on several individual tasks and even on mean accuracy at some pruning ratios (e.g., 10% and partially at 30%), which undercuts the claim that RCPU "consistently outperforms" FLAP.

Many reported improvements are very small in absolute terms (e.g., PPL 13.55 vs 13.52, or 14.40 vs 14.55) with no reported variance, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds/calibration-set samples, making it hard to assess statistical significance of the claimed gains.

The scaled variant (Rot.+Scale) is introduced but shown to provide only marginal, inconsistent benefit, raising the question of why this variant is included as a main contribution rather than as a minor extension or omitted.

Compensation is restricted to o_proj and down_proj only; other projections (q/k/v/gate/up) are pruned but not compensated, and this design choice, while empirically justified for these two layers, is not tested at the full-model level with all pruned layers compensated, leaving open whether further gains (or drawbacks) exist.

The method is layer-wise and greedy with no joint optimization or analysis of error accumulation/propagation across many layers in deep transformer stacks, which could be more consequential in larger models.

Robustness to calibration set size (beyond the standard 128 samples) is not studied, despite the paper's central motivating claim being about overfitting under limited calibration data — a controlled study varying calibration size would substantiate this claim much more convincingly.

No exploration of combining RCPU's rotation-based correction with FLAP's bias-based correction, despite the paper noting these approaches address different aspects of the error (directional vs. mean), which seems like a natural and potentially stronger extension left unexplored.

strengths: The core idea—formulating post-pruning error compensation as an Orthogonal Procrustes problem to preserve norms/inner products of output representations—is well-motivated and technically clean, with a closed-form solution (SVD-based) that is easy to implement.
The paper clearly articulates the failure mode of unconstrained least-squares compensation (overfitting/geometric distortion under small calibration sets) and provides a principled remedy.
The variance-aware column scoring is a simple, intuitive extension of WANDA-sp that is easy to combine with the rotation update.

Useful ablations are included: comparison of rotation-only vs. least-squares compensation (Fig. 2), where-to-apply-rotation analysis (Table 3), and efficiency/overhead measurements (Table 4), which help clarify the mechanism and practical cost of the method.
The method is training-free, requires no architectural changes, and integrates directly into an existing structured pruning pipeline (Wanda-sp style), which is practically appealing.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to a single model (LLaMA-7B); there is no evidence the method generalizes to other model families/sizes (e.g., OPT, LLaMA-13B/70B, Mistral), which is a significant limitation for claims of general applicability in structured pruning.

Baselines are narrow: only WANDA-sp and FLAP are compared quantitatively, despite the related-work section discussing stronger/more relevant training-free structured pruning methods such as SliceGPT, which is not empirically compared even though it is directly relevant (both use orthogonal transformations).

The claimed 'consistent' improvement over FLAP is not fully supported by Table 2: at several pruning ratios RCPU underperforms FLAP on individual tasks (e.g., BoolQ at 30%: 61.25 vs 66.67; ARC-e at 20% and 30%), and mean accuracy gains are often marginal (e.g., 56.34 vs 56.20 at 30%), weakening the strength of the central empirical claim.

The reduction in 'degrees of freedom' from constraining A to an orthogonal Q is somewhat overstated — Q still has O(d_out^2/2) parameters (thousands for LLaMA-7B's hidden size), so the paper does not adequately analyze or empirically demonstrate that the Procrustes fit itself is well-conditioned/non-overfitting given the small calibration set (128 samples), beyond indirect PPL evidence.

No error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing are reported; all results appear to be single-run point estimates, making it hard to assess whether the (often small) reported gains are robust.

The variance-aware score's contribution is not cleanly isolated in the main tables (Tables 1 and 2 conflate score choice and compensation method); a direct ablation isolating the scoring rule's effect on accuracy (not just PPL in Fig. 2) is missing.

The efficiency analysis only reports per-layer pruning time, not end-to-end pruning time or memory overhead for the whole model, limiting insight into scalability to larger models where the paper claims practical applicability.
